claims.statement: Talon wires one `talon_mcp_middleware()` into the main `DeepAgentRuntime` and installs the same middleware in freshly compiled local subagents, so both paths receive the MCP adapter behavior.

`load_mcp_tools()` discovers each configured server through `MCPAdapter`, prefixes discovered tool names with the server name, and marks their metadata as Talon MCP tools; `skillOnly` servers receive an additional metadata marker.

For OpenAI Responses API model requests, Talon's MCP middleware converts only marked MCP `BaseTool` values with `convert_to_openai_tool(..., strict=False)` and otherwise leaves the request tools unchanged; non-Responses models are passed through.

For a marked MCP invocation, the middleware removes only optional empty string arguments for string-like or unspecified properties, retains required empty strings and explicitly non-string properties, and invokes the handler under the exact tool-call ID as authorization context, restoring that context afterward.

The middleware converts an `MCPError` into an error `ToolMessage` correlated to the original tool name and tool-call ID and exposes only the code and message, while non-MCP errors propagate through the normal runtime path.

Talon has no MCP elicitation UI: recognized elicitation interrupts are resumed with a cancel action for each valid request key, while malformed elicitation payloads are rejected instead of being processed as approval requests.

MCP refresh is serialized and revision-driven; the runtime retains its prior graph after a refresh failure, while successful replacement builds a new graph, so running work retains the capabilities of the graph it began with.

Talon selects its MCP config from `DEEPAGENTS_TALON_MCP_CONFIG` or `~/.deepagents/.mcp.json`, validates and expands server definitions, supports stdio, SSE, and streamable HTTP transports, and records individual server load failures as status outcomes so sibling servers can still load.

Focused Talon tests exercise middleware argument and authorization handling, protocol-error behavior, Responses schema preservation and real-adapter invocation, elicitation cancellation, in-flight reload behavior, stdio lifecycle, and skill-scoped MCP disclosure.

`MCPConfigStore` exposes a redacted configuration view with an HMAC revision and an update capability that locks, rereads, compare-and-swaps the revision, validates a single-server replacement, writes atomically, and schedules refresh only after a successful write.

Configuration reads redact stored strings except allowed enum values and exact environment references, preserve unseen unmanaged fields across supported updates, and return generic errors rather than file contents; this mediation is not filesystem isolation because Talon's execution-capable shell can bypass it.

When an update reuses a `<redacted>` stored value without active approval, Talon rejects any changed managed routing or execution setting except tool filters, preventing a restored credential from being redirected; a required approval policy permits the human-reviewed update.

Disabled MCP servers are not environment-expanded, connected, or offered authentication; toggling `enabled` through the configuration store schedules refresh and unloads or restores their tools after the provider refreshes.

Fresh local subagents receive only applicable approval rules and add `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` when such rules exist, whereas Talon refuses precompiled subagents because approval policy cannot be enforced within them.
A senderless Telegram channel post cannot create a pending tool approval, even when the channel exposure mode otherwise admits that conversation.

The CLI builds the model-backed runtime from MCP tools and callbacks, subagent/cron/checkpoint configuration, Talon MCP middleware, and an optional sandbox; it installs the persistent scheduler only when channels are configured and routes job execution and delivery through the host.

TalonHost starts the runtime before bound channels and scheduler, unwinds a failed partial startup, and on shutdown cancels work before stopping channels, scheduler, and runtime while continuing after component-stop failures.

`AgentRequest` carries host-supplied metadata and optional interaction handlers, while `AgentResult` carries acknowledged background IDs so the host can requeue results if it cannot deliver the reply.

DeepAgentRuntime builds a graph from Talon's filesystem, model, progress, approval, hook, task, background, skill, and supplied middleware; it removes skill-only MCP tools from the ordinary tool list and configures local subagents from the available catalog.

Each runtime invocation captures graph and approval snapshots under a tools lock; reload failure preserves the prior graph and replacement builds a graph before assignment, so an in-flight turn is not changed by a reload.
TalonHost serializes messages by provider-qualified conversation root and processes commands, pending approvals, authorization callbacks, and pending questions before an ordinary replacement turn.
Approval and question replies require and bind to an identified sender, while unattended background-delivery requests receive no approval, authorization, or question handler.
Runtime approval authority is disabled for cron and background-delivery requests, and invocation-scoped state is reset after execution.

Background subagents are in-memory, conversation-owned jobs with shared capacity; workers clear authorization and approval authority, safely convert failures and approval interrupts to bounded results, and restrict management to the owning conversation.

The host dispatches completed background results only for eligible conversations with exponential backoff and uses an unattended follow-up turn; acknowledged IDs are requeued when its reply was not delivered.
Cron delegation runs inline with a separate semaphore and timeout, forbids nested delegation, and returns a safe tool error on failure or timeout.
Opt-in activity logging emits structured, bounded, redacted run/model/tool events; LangSmith tracing requires an explicit flag and API key, and observability failures do not prevent cancellation.
Host and observability tests cover lifecycle/routing/interaction seams, trace opt-in, and logging redaction.
